about.purpose: Selector map that re-scopes the React Button's OWN compiled CSS onto the legacy classic-admin button classes, so classic wp-admin renders identically to the React component. This is the single source of the generation step (generate.mjs).
about.source: packages/components/build-style/style.css — every rule whose selector starts with `.components-button` is extracted and its selector rewritten via the map below. Declarations are taken verbatim (already token-based), so classic gets React's exact implementation, including the transparent-border + outline/outline-offset focus construction.
about.contract: Legacy selectors and markup (.button, .button-primary, .wp-core-ui, get_submit_button() output) are preserved; only React's declarations are re-pointed onto them.

stateClassMap.__doc: Core drives button state from CLASSES as well as pseudo-classes, because legacy admin JS toggles them directly. React has no equivalent concept, so each rule carrying one of these pseudos also emits a class form built from the SAME declarations — the class-driven states then render identically to React rather than merely being present. Only a top-level pseudo on the subject is swapped; guards inside `:not(...)` survive untouched.

stateClassVariantMap.__doc: Extra legacy class forms for a state that exist only for certain variants. Core writes these as bare selectors (`.wp-core-ui .button-disabled`), but always applies them to an element that ALSO carries `.button`, so they are APPENDED to the mapped subject rather than replacing it. Appending is not cosmetic: our re-scoped base rule uses `:is()`/`:not()` and so outranks Core original specificity, and a bare `.button-disabled` would silently lose the colour battle to it. Not emitted for the link variant: classic has no link equivalent, and it would leak link styling onto every disabled button.

stateClassNotMapped.:active: DELIBERATELY NOT MAPPED to `.active`. In classic admin the two are different states: `:active` is the transient mouse-down state, while `.active` is a PERSISTENT `selected setting` (the segmented-control pressed state), which Core styles with an extra inset shadow and outline. Mapping them together looks plausible in a screenshot but silently breaks every segmented control. `.active` stays in buttons-exceptions.css until React's `is-pressed` is deliberately mapped onto it and the visual change is recorded.

height.why: 40px is always the default button size (Joen's ruling). React's base height is 36px with 40px behind `.is-next-40px-default-size`; classic has no such class, so we fold 40px into the base and drop the opt-in rule. Excludes small (24px), compact (32px) and hero (48px) so those keep their own heights, and excludes link (auto height). The exclusions are load-bearing: this selector's :is()/:not() specificity beats the plain compound in buttons-exceptions.css, so a size omitted here is silently forced to 40px no matter what the exceptions file says.

focusBoxShadowReset.why: The per-scheme `colors` stylesheet (still enqueued for admin chrome) paints a LEGACY box-shadow focus ring on buttons. We adopt React's outline/outline-offset focus, so neutralise the box-shadow to avoid a double ring. Our stylesheet loads after `colors`, so `box-shadow: none` wins by source order.

dropped.note: React selectors with no classic equivalent are dropped. Core's buttons.css is dequeued, so a dropped case is genuinely unstyled unless a classic supplement covers it — see the coverage gaps in README.md.

selectors.reason: Classic uses `.button-link-delete`, which has no React equivalent. Currently unstyled under the dequeue — needs porting.
React-only busy animation class; classic markup has no `.is-busy`.
React icon-slot layout; classic `<input type=submit>` cannot host icon children. Icon buttons handled separately.
React uses `.dashicon`; classic uses `.dashicons` (plural). Different class; left to Core.
